documents.unit: Academic Affairs Division / Office of the Provost
documents.title: UL Lafayette Guidance on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom
documents.summary: University-wide guidance from the Provost's office that applies to coursework and leaves the AI rule to colleges, departments and faculty. It lists areas a course policy should cover (permitted uses, responsible use and citation, penalties) and offers three sample syllabus statements.
documents.stance_why: Document sets no university-wide stance: it says it "encourages academic colleges, departments, and individual faculty to develop specific policies" and that faculty "will be the ones to determine what constitutes proper use of GAI". It offers three sample syllabus statements (prohibiting, mixed, encouraging), so it is delegates with those templates as tiers.

units.why: Opening framing: "The proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools is rapidly changing higher education"; context for the guidance, so an institutional-framework statement (P56), informs.
units.anchor: The proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools is rapidly changing higher education.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this sentence; coder A skipped it. Source text confirms it is the document's opening premise and explains why guidance is needed, so kept as framing (P56).

units.why: GAI "can answer questions, formulate problems, serve as a brainstorming partner" and "fuel innovation": names benefits of AI without a rule, so P87.
units.anchor: serve as a brainstorming partner
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. The source lists benefits (answers questions, brainstorming partner, innovation), which is what P87 covers; kept.

units.why: States "AI can also deliver results that contain significant inaccuracies and conscious and unconscious biases": output is unreliable, so P31; the bias mention is secondary.
units.anchor: AI can also deliver results that contain significant inaccuracies and conscious and unconscious biases
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type, actor, phase and modality; differed only in topic labels. Final uses codebook topic names.
units.fit_note: Also names bias as a concern; framed here as unreliability of output.

units.why: Says the university "is training the future workforce" that is "increasingly exposed to and engaging with Generative AI tools": a workforce-readiness reason to engage with AI (P44), spoken by the university, so admin.
units.anchor: a workforce that is increasingly exposed to and engaging with Generative AI tools
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P44. Actor differed (A admin, B all). The sentence is the university speaking about its own role ("the University of Louisiana at Lafayette is training"), so admin.
units.fit_note: Says the workforce uses AI; does not say courses must teach AI use.

units.why: "we now do so in an academic ecosystem where GAI is an undeniable presence" acknowledges AI cannot be avoided; a framing premise, informs.
units.anchor: we now do so in an academic ecosystem where GAI is an undeniable presence
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this, as P82. The text says AI is "undeniable", not that use cannot be prevented or verified (P82's definition), so P82 would stretch; coded as framework premise P56. Kept as a real framing statement.
units.fit_note: Close to P82 (acknowledging AI cannot be avoided) but the text does not mention prevention or verification.

units.why: "It is our responsibility to ensure that we engage with AI in a manner that safeguards academic integrity" gives integrity as the ground for AI rules (P95), spoken by the university.
units.anchor: engage with AI in a manner that safeguards academic integrity
units.resolution_why: A coded P95 (integrity as the reason), B coded P56 (principle). The sentence states the reason for the AI rules as safeguarding academic integrity, which is P95's definition; P56 fits less well because no framework is set up here. Modality informs (A) over should (B): it states a responsibility as rationale, with no instruction to anyone.

units.why: Scope sentence: "applies to student intellectual coursework products at the graduate and undergraduate levels" defines what the guidance covers.
units.anchor: applies to student intellectual coursework products at the graduate and undergraduate levels
units.resolution_why: A coded P56, B coded P61. The sentence defines the policy's scope, which is P61's definition; P56 is for framework or principle statements.
units.fit_note: Defines scope but not AI itself.

units.why: Purpose sentence: "to promote ethical engagement with AI across the University" states the guidance's purpose, a framework-level principle (P56).
units.anchor: promote ethical engagement with AI across the University
units.resolution_why: Type agreed. Unit stance differed (A neutral, B encourage). The sentence states a purpose, not a call for AI use, so neutral.

units.why: "encourages academic colleges, departments, and individual faculty to develop specific policies" hands rule-setting to units below the university (P85); the faculty-only decision is coded separately as P04.
units.anchor: encourages academic colleges, departments, and individual faculty to develop specific policies for their students
units.resolution_why: Both coders gave P85 and the same codes.
units.fit_note: Also names individual faculty (P04).

units.why: Rules vary "depending on the skills and learning outcomes they seek to impart", tying AI decisions to learning outcomes (P83).
units.anchor: depending on the skills and learning outcomes they seek to impart

units.why: Ethical engagement with GAI, "including restrictions, guardrails, or complete integration of GAI into assignments, will vary significantly across disciplines, and even among classes": the rule differs by course (P04).
units.anchor: restrictions, guardrails, or complete integration of GAI into assignments, will vary significantly
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this clause (A merged it into the P83 unit). It states a separate fact, that AI rules range from restriction to complete integration and vary by discipline and class, so kept as its own unit.

units.why: "All faculty have academic freedom in their classrooms and will be the ones to determine what constitutes proper use of GAI" places the decision with each instructor (P04); no university default is set.
units.anchor: will be the ones to determine what constitutes proper use of GAI in their classroom

units.why: "it is the students' responsibility to familiarize themselves with relevant expectations and policies": students must learn each course's rules (P78).
units.anchor: it is the students’ responsibility to familiarize themselves with relevant expectations and policies

units.why: "Because different classes may have different AI policies" states that a course's AI policy is particular to that class (P11).
units.anchor: Because different classes may have different AI policies
units.policy: Different classes may have different AI policies.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this clause (A coded the whole sentence once, as P78). It states a distinct fact (policies differ by class) from the student duty, so kept as its own unit.
units.fit_note: Says policies differ across classes, not explicitly that permissions do not carry over.

units.why: Instructors should "Define the range of uses of AI and be explicit about what you allow in your class": state expectations explicitly (P09).
units.anchor: be explicit about what you allow in your class
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A course-start, B before-course). The instruction is to communicate the allowed uses to the class, which is expectation-setting, so course-start.

units.why: Example use "brainstorm and conduct preliminary research for assignments"; brainstorming is P15. It is listed among uses a course policy could define.
units.anchor: Use of GAI to brainstorm and conduct preliminary research for assignments
units.policy: Course policies may define as a permitted use: GAI to brainstorm and conduct preliminary research for assignments.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type, actor and modality. The anchor alone does not state a modality, so the normalized policy relies on the surrounding list ("Define the range of uses of AI ... Some examples include"). Phase set to course-start because the list is about what a course policy states.
units.fit_note: Also names preliminary research, which P15 does not mention.

units.why: Example use "summarize articles and other readings" is a study aid (P14). It is listed among uses a course policy could define.
units.anchor: Use of GAI to summarize articles and other readings
units.policy: Course policies may define as a permitted use: GAI to summarize articles and other readings.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type, actor and modality. The anchor alone does not state a modality, so the normalized policy relies on the surrounding list ("Define the range of uses of AI ... Some examples include"). Phase set to course-start because the list is about what a course policy states.

units.why: Example use "analyze quantitative or qualitative data" matches P89. It is listed among uses a course policy could define.
units.anchor: Use of GAI to analyze quantitative or qualitative data
units.policy: Course policies may define as a permitted use: GAI to analyze quantitative or qualitative data.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type, actor and modality. The anchor alone does not state a modality, so the normalized policy relies on the surrounding list ("Define the range of uses of AI ... Some examples include"). Phase set to course-start because the list is about what a course policy states.

units.why: Example use "proof-reading, grammar assistance, or to adjust style and tone" is editing support (P91). It is listed among uses a course policy could define.
units.anchor: Use of GAI for proof-reading, grammar assistance, or to adjust style and tone
units.policy: Course policies may define as a permitted use: GAI for proof-reading, grammar assistance, or to adjust style and tone.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on type, actor and modality. The anchor alone does not state a modality, so the normalized policy relies on the surrounding list ("Define the range of uses of AI ... Some examples include"). Phase set to course-start because the list is about what a course policy states.

units.why: Example use "develop graphics or foreign language translations" is listed as a use a course policy could allow.
units.anchor: Use of GAI to develop graphics or foreign language translations
units.policy: Course policies may define as a permitted use: GAI to develop graphics or foreign language translations.
units.resolution_why: A coded P18 (prose tools incl. translation) with a fit note; B coded UNCOVERED. P18 is about prose and writing rules separate from code; graphics generation is not prose and translation is only half of the unit, so P18 would be a stretch. Left UNCOVERED per the codebook.
units.uncovered_note: AI may be used to create graphics or translations for coursework.

units.why: Example use of a "draft or outline of a work product that is critically edited and expanded upon by the student": AI-produced draft allowed if the student edits it, closest to P91.
units.anchor: outline of a work product that is critically edited and expanded upon by the student
units.policy: Course policies may define as a permitted use: GAI to produce a draft or outline of a work product that is critically edited and expanded upon by the student.
units.resolution_why: Both coders gave P91 with the same fit concern.
units.fit_note: AI produces the draft or outline itself and the student then edits and expands it, which is more than editing one's own writing.

units.why: "Reaffirm that students are responsible for accuracy, bias, and integrity of any use of GAI" tells instructors to restate student responsibility for AI output (P29).
units.anchor: students are responsible for accuracy, bias, and integrity of any use of GAI
units.resolution_why: A and B agreed on P29 and all codes.
units.fit_note: Responsibility is for accuracy, bias and integrity of AI use, not ownership of the work as such.

units.why: Instructors should articulate AI's limitations and students' "responsibility to fact-check AI for both accuracy and bias in results" (P31).
units.anchor: responsibility to fact-check AI for both accuracy and bias in results

units.why: "Define the importance of being transparent about AI usage" tells instructors to explain why transparency matters, a disclosure-related instruction (P24).
units.anchor: Define the importance of being transparent about AI usage
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this sentence; A skipped it. It is a separate sentence from the citation requirement, so kept.
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to explain transparency rather than requiring a statement.

units.why: "For courses where students may use GAI, require citations where there is AI usage" is a disclosure-with-submission rule (P24) addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: require citations where there is AI usage

units.why: Alternative documentation: "saving and uploading for instructor review transcripts of GAI interaction, or screenshots of GAI sessions" (P26).
units.anchor: saving and uploading for instructor review transcripts of GAI interaction
units.resolution_why: Unit stance differed (A permit, B neutral). The sentence offers a documentation method and takes no position on AI use itself, so neutral.

units.why: "encourage students to participate in trainings that teach proper AI usage" is AI training for students (P70).
units.anchor: encourage students to participate in trainings that teach proper AI usage

units.why: Penalties should "Be specific about how these apply to different types of AI, potentially differentiating between grammar/punctuation assistance GAI and other forms": the instruction is to make penalties specific, so P37.
units.anchor: differentiating between grammar/punctuation assistance GAI and other forms of GAI
units.resolution_why: A coded P100 (routine features exempt), B coded P37 (state penalties in advance). The sentence sits under "Articulate penalties" and only suggests differentiating grammar assistance, without exempting it, so the instruction is about how specific penalties are, which is P37. P100 is not assigned because no exemption is stated.
units.fit_note: Also touches the routine-feature distinction (P100), but does not exempt grammar assistance.

units.why: "then the use of GAI in that course constitutes academic misconduct" when AI is not permitted: unauthorized AI use is classed as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: then the use of GAI in that course constitutes academic misconduct
units.resolution_why: Type agreed. Actor differed (A student, B all); the consequence binds students who use AI where it is not permitted, so student.

units.why: The same sentence defines what the ban covers: AI used "to author or assist with any portion of the final assignments or intellectual scaffolding leading up to it" is barred where AI is not permitted (P19).
units.anchor: author or assist with any portion of the final assignments or intellectual scaffolding
units.frag_start: to author or assist with any portion
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this as its own unit; A folded it into the misconduct unit. The scope of the ban (assistance and scaffolding, not only final text) is a separate rule from the misconduct classification, so kept.
units.fit_note: Extends the prohibition to assistance and preliminary scaffolding.

units.why: "Indicate grade penalties (if applicable) clearly and specifically" asks instructors to state penalties in advance (P37).
units.anchor: Indicate grade penalties (if applicable) clearly and specifically

units.why: Under "Resources for instructors" the page links citation guides (APA, MLA, Chicago) and "Sample Assignments redesigned to incorporate GAI": resources supporting instructors (P63).
units.anchor: Sample Assignments redesigned to incorporate GAI
units.frag_start: How to Cite ChatGPT from the APA
units.resolution_why: A coded P35 (redesign assignments) on the link title, B coded P63 (support for instructors) on the section. The text is a list of resource links with no rule about redesigning assignments, so P35 overstates; P63 fits the section.
units.fit_note: Resources are sample assignments and citation guides, not workshops; the redesign link gives no detail.

units.why: Sample prohibiting statement: "Use of artificial intelligence (AI) to generate material is strictly prohibited" bans AI for course work.
units.anchor: Use of artificial intelligence (AI) to generate material is strictly prohibited
units.resolution_why: A coded P19, B coded P01. This is a blanket ban on AI-generated material for the course (a default prohibition), which is P01; the narrower P19 (do not submit AI-produced work) is coded on the later sentence about edited AI material. B's frag_start pointed at the preceding sentence and was replaced.

units.why: "All work submitted for this course must be your own original production" is an ownership rule (P29).
units.anchor: All work submitted for this course must be your own original production
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this sentence; B skipped it. It is a separate requirement in the sample prohibiting statement, so kept.

units.why: Sample says AI-generated submissions "will be considered a violation of the University's academic integrity policy" (P36).
units.anchor: will be considered a violation of the University’s academic integrity policy

units.why: "This includes AI-generated material that you have summarized or edited" extends the ban to edited AI output (P19).
units.anchor: This includes AI-generated material that you have summarized or edited

units.why: "This excludes AI-supported tools providing spelling and grammar checks" exempts routine features from the ban (P100).
units.anchor: This excludes AI-supported tools providing spelling and grammar checks

units.why: Sample mixed statement: "you may use generative AI tools for brainstorming and research" allows brainstorming (P15).
units.anchor: you may use generative AI tools for brainstorming and research
units.policy: Students may use generative AI tools for brainstorming and research.
units.resolution_why: Both gave P15; A's normalized policy kept because the anchor omits the subject and context.
units.fit_note: Also allows research, beyond brainstorming.

units.why: The same sample says students "must develop and compose your final assignments independently", barring AI authorship of final work (P19).
units.anchor: must develop and compose your final assignments independently
units.policy: Students must develop and compose their final assignments independently.

units.why: "If you have questions or suggestions for potential exceptions, please email me" invites students to ask the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: If you have questions or suggestions for potential exceptions, please email me
units.resolution_why: A: course-start, may. B: during-work, should. The sentence is an open invitation to raise questions or exception requests while doing the work, not an instruction, so may and during-work.
units.fit_note: Also invites suggestions for exceptions, not only asking when unsure.

units.why: Sample encouraging statement: "Use of artificial intelligence (AI) to generate a first draft of an assignment is permitted" allows AI-drafted assignment text, a prose-drafting permission (P18); the review condition is coded separately.
units.anchor: Use of artificial intelligence (AI) to generate a first draft of an assignment is permitted
units.policy: AI may be used to generate a first draft of an assignment.
units.resolution_why: A coded P18, B coded P16 (AI-generated code). The sentence concerns drafts of assignments in general, not code, so P16 does not fit; P18 (prose and writing rules) is the nearest.
units.fit_note: Permission for AI-drafted assignment text; P18 is about prose rules in general.

units.why: "you must review and revise any AI-generated material before submission" is a condition on the allowed first draft; students must check and fix AI output (P31).
units.anchor: you must review and revise any AI-generated material before submission
units.frag_start: but you must review and revise
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this as a separate unit (A put it inside its first-draft policy text). It is a distinct requirement, so kept.
units.fit_note: Review and revise requirement rather than a fact-check requirement.

units.why: "You are responsible for the content of any work submitted for this course" is a responsibility rule (P29).
units.anchor: You are responsible for the content of any work submitted for this course

units.why: "you are required to be transparent about your use of AI-generated material by following citation and documentation guidelines" is a disclosure requirement (P24).
units.anchor: you are required to be transparent about your use of AI-generated material

units.why: Warns that AI generators "are prone to factual errors, incorrect or fabricated citations, and misinterpretations", so output must be checked (P31).
units.anchor: they are prone to factual errors, incorrect or fabricated citations

documents.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines
documents.summary: Short Graduate School page framing generative AI in research, teaching and communication around transparency, faculty involvement and ethical use. It names concerns such as authorial consent and intellectual property and links to other university guidance; it gives few concrete rules. The linked guidelines document was not in the saved text.
documents.stance_why: The page frames GAI use in scholarly work around "transparency, faculty involvement, and ethical use" and says GAI "can enhance research, teaching, and communication" provided it is used responsibly and "paired with expertise and integrity". It bans nothing and delegates nothing explicitly, so AI is allowed with conditions (permit). Coder B coded delegates; the saved text never hands the decision to instructors or courses, so delegates is not supported. Weak stance: the page is mostly framing.

units.why: "committed to preparing the next generation of researchers with integrity and ethical awareness" is a framework-level purpose statement by the university (P56).
units.anchor: committed to preparing the next generation of researchers with integrity and ethical awareness
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A all, B admin). The university states its own commitment, so admin.

units.why: "it is essential to use these tools responsibly" as GAI enters "research, teaching, and communication": a general responsible-use principle (P56).
units.anchor: it is essential to use these tools responsibly
units.resolution_why: Both coded P56 should; A's extra normalized policy dropped because the anchor states the principle on its own.

units.why: "emphasizes transparency, faculty involvement, and ethical use in scholarly work" states the principles for scholarly AI use (P62); no concrete rule is given.
units.anchor: emphasizes transparency, faculty involvement, and ethical use in scholarly work
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A student, B all). The text addresses the community without naming students, so all.
units.fit_note: States principles for scholarly work but gives no concrete rule on theses or manuscripts.

units.why: Names concerns of "authorial consent, intellectual property, and academic integrity"; closest type is P52 (IP).
units.anchor: authorial consent, intellectual property, and academic integrity
units.resolution_why: Both coded P52 with the same fit concern.
units.fit_note: Also names authorial consent and academic integrity; no specific copyright rule is given.

units.why: "ensuring that GAI supports research rather than replacing the critical insight and creativity of human scholars": AI should not replace human thinking (P32).
units.anchor: GAI supports research rather than replacing the critical insight and creativity of human scholars
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A student, B all); the sentence is general about scholars, so all.

units.why: "These guidelines help ensure that AI is used ethically and effectively, paired with expertise and integrity": AI should be paired with human expertise (P32).
units.anchor: paired with expertise and integrity
units.resolution_why: A coded this closing sentence as should; B anchored the preceding clause ("cannot replicate human creativity, insight, or judgment") as informs. They cover the same closing passage. The clause about limits is rationale and the "paired with" part is the normative one, so should on the "paired with" anchor.
units.fit_note: Asks that AI be paired with expertise and integrity; does not say who decides.

notes: Distance Learning 'AI Tools & Use' page not found (louisiana.edu/distancelearning/technology saved only navigation). Office of Communications & Marketing AI guidelines exist but are not about teaching/learning. No College of Engineering or School of Computing and Informatics AI policy found. Graduate School page links to a separate Graduate School GAI Guidelines document that was not in the saved text, so only visible principles were coded. Reconciler dropped coder B's P85 unit on the Graduate School page's list of links to other offices' guidance (navigation, not a policy statement).
